title: The ripe olive
hookLine: Marcus pictures an olive falling ripe, blessing the tree that bore it (Meditations 4.48)

lines: A SOFT TAP ON THE GROUND.
cards: If you've ever stood under an olive tree in the fall, in Greece or Italy or California, you might have seen it: fruit dropping on its own, a soft tap on the ground, then another. Nobody shook the branch.
The olive was simply ready. Around the ancient Mediterranean, the olive was everywhere: food, lamp oil, medicine, the oil rubbed on athletes.
And in book four of his notebook, at the end of a long, sober passage, Marcus reaches for one to say something hard in a gentle way.

teach.b: Marcus lists people who are gone: doctors who frowned over many patients and then died themselves, astrologers who predicted others' deaths, philosophers who argued about immortality, great generals, whole cities.
He isn't being morbid. He's reminding himself, again, how short and shared a human life is. Second, the olive.

teach.h: FALL LIKE A RIPE OLIVE, GRATEFUL.
teach.b: Pass through this little space of time in keeping with nature, he writes, and end the journey content, the way a ripe olive falls, blessing nature that produced it and thanking the tree it grew on.
A falling olive doesn't cling. It doesn't curse the branch. It drops in its season, grateful.

teach.h: EVERYTHING IN NATURE HAS ITS TIME.
teach.b: For Marcus, everything in nature has its time: being young, growing up, getting gray, and also dying. Elsewhere he calls death one of the works of nature, like teething or a beard coming in.
Some people find comfort in that; others find it hard. Both are honest reactions, and the Meditations don't demand that you feel one way about it. Fourth, the smaller lesson.

teach.h: IN SEASON: NOT EARLY, NOT LATE.
teach.b: The olive is in season: not early, not forced, not late, and it gives thanks for what grew it.
Marcus means it as a way to end. It can also be a way to eat: a fruit picked in its own month carries the weather and the soil of the place it came from.

how: Some readers of Marcus use the image of the ripe olive to reflect on accepting life's seasons, and to eat food in season with attention and thanks.

o: an olive picked early so it keeps on the shelf
Marcus's picture of a life ending in season, grateful
a sign of plenty, promising a good harvest ahead

s: in Meditations 4.48, the olive falls cursing the branch
it falls blessing nature and thanking the tree it grew on.
Marcus compares death to natural events like teething or growing a beard
he treats it as one of the works of nature.
the olive image comes at the end of a list of people who have died
doctors, astrologers, philosophers, generals, whole cities.

games.q: you're Marcus, writing about how short life is. how do you end the thought?
o: with a warning to fear death
with an olive falling ripe, grateful to the tree
with advice to live forever through fame
games.why: he ends with a ripe olive falling, blessing nature and thanking the tree that bore it.

practice: Hold something in season, a piece of fruit, a vegetable, a handful of nuts, or picture one, and think of the plant it came from, the weather that ripened it, the hands that picked and carried it.
If it's in front of you, taste it slowly. Let one silent thank-you go back to the tree, the field or the people, and sit with the taste.

wordCard.voice: Ripe olive, Marcus's picture of a life that ends in its season, falling without clinging, grateful to the tree that bore it. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: olive, the fruit and the tree.
